agent_notes: The superscription (תְּפִלָּה לְמֹשֶׁה אִישׁ־הָאֱלֹהִים) is counted as part of verse 1 here, as in the Hebrew numbering; the KJV prints it as verse 0. The preposition lamed in 'lemosheh' is rendered 'of Moses'; Meiri on Psalms 90:1 records the reading 'for the sons of Moses', which I did not follow.

Pos 6 ma'on glossed 'a dwelling' (STEPBible 'a dwelling place'). Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as a place of refuge. In the commentary I cite Deuteronomy 33:27 as an echo; that is my own reading, not a packet citation.

history.note: [consider] Say that the KJV sets the title apart as an unnumbered heading, so verse 1 in both counts begins 'Lord'; and 'the address opens with Adonai'. (PS.90.1: KJV (90:0, 90:1) 'A Prayer of Moses the man of God. Lord, thou hast been...')

agent_notes: 'rahbam' glossed 'their bluster/pride'. KJV 'strength' is a guess; ASV 'pride' follows the root rhb 'to be arrogant, to rage'. Metzudat Zion cites Isaiah 3:5 for 'ירהבו'. The dating of 70/80 years against Moses' 120 years is addressed by Ibn Ezra and Meiri; I mention it in the commentary without committing.

Second half of the verse is syntactically obscure: 'ukhe-yir'atekha evratekha' lit. 'and as your fear [is] your fury'. Versions split: KJV 'according to thy fear, so is thy wrath'; ASV 'according to the fear that is due unto thee'; YLT keeps the question. I kept a short, ambiguous English that does not choose.
Pos 5 glossed 'and we will bring' (STEPBible 'so we may bring'). Rashi's reading of 'ken' as the numeral kaf-nun = 70 is mentioned in the commentary as a classical reading only.

שׁוּבָה is glossed 'turn back / return' (not STEPBible's bare 'return') because Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David all read it as 'turn back from your burning anger'; the Hebrew itself names no 'from what'. The classical comments say so; the verb stands bare in the text.

The five English versions split on והנחם: KJV/ASV/Webster 'let it repent thee', YLT 'repent', BBE 'let your purpose be changed'. I keep the reflexive-passive sense (Niphal imperative, 'let yourself be sorry / relent') and give the same verb nacham as Moses uses in Exod 32:12, 14; that cross-reference is my own reading, not drawn from the packet.

Meiri and Ibn Ezra take 'in the morning' as youth, Rashi and Radak as the dawn of deliverance, Metzudat David as 'every morning'. I keep the literal 'in the morning' and note the readings in the commentary rather than choosing one.

Radak rejects the midrashic reading that the days of joy must equal the days of exile in number; I keep the neutral 'according to the days' and mention both readings. The form כִּימוֹת is a rarer plural of 'days' (yamot rather than yamim).
STEPBible glosses פָעֳלֶךָ as 'deed[s]'; the form is singular ('your work'), matching the singular verb יֵרָאֶה. I use 'your work'.

Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read the doubled 'establish the work of our hands' as emphasis; Rashi cites a tradition tying it to two blessings (Tabernacle and ordinary labour). Malbim's long comment on Moses's own situation I cite only in part. The sense of נֹעַם (pleasantness, favour, beauty) is where the versions split: KJV/Webster 'beauty', ASV 'favor', BBE 'pleasure'. I choose 'sweetness' in the literal layer to show its root meaning of pleasantness, and 'favor' in the dramatic layer.

history.note: [consider] Use 'upon us' (or 'for us') in the dramatic layer rather than 'beneath us', and gloss pos 9 the same way as the literal layer. (PS.90.17: 'כּוֹנְנָה עָלֵינוּ'; KJV 'establish thou the work of our hands upon us'.)

agent_notes: Reviewer request applied: the 'back to the dust' reading is now attributed to Ibn Ezra and Meiri, the repentance reading to Radak, Rashi and Metzudat David, and the KJV sentence rewritten to say that shuvu, like 'return', can carry both senses.

dakka' (H1793B) glossed 'crushed matter', after STEPBible. The literal layer keeps 'crushed [thing]' rather than 'dust', because the parallel with Gen 3:19 'to dust you shall return' is an inference, not in the word itself. The five English versions split: KJV and ASV 'destruction', YLT 'a bruised thing', BBE 'his dust'. Rashi and Radak read the word as a state of crushedness (old age, affliction), which fits the root dk' 'crush'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri read verse 3b as a return to dust; both readings are given.
The Targum's 'on account of his sin' (על חוביה) is not cited as a source for the lexical claims; it is a paraphrase that moves the verse toward repentance.

(PS.90.3 packet: Radak 'ותאמר שובו בני אדם. שישובו בני אדם בתשובה'; Ibn Ezra 'אל העפר אשר לקחתם ממנה'; Meiri '[ותגזור שישובו בני אדם אל עפרם]'.)
[consider] Keep one verdict: the KJV is faithful apart from the supplied 'but'. (PS.90.4 KJV: 'are but as yesterday when it is past'.)

agent_notes: The verse is hard. 'zeramtam' is read as 'you sweep them away [as with a flood]' (zerem 'downpour'); 'shenah' as 'sleep'. 'yachalof' can mean 'passes on' or 'sprouts anew' (cf. Job 14:7, cited by Meiri and Ibn Ezra on verse 6). I translated 'passes on' in the literal layer and kept the double sense in the notes. I did not follow the STEPBible gloss for pos 6 ('[which] it sprouts up') in the literal layer. The Isaiah 40:31 cross-reference in the commentary comes from Metzudat Zion's 'yachalifu koach'; the packet gives no chapter number for it. Rashi's text is cut off mid-sentence in the packet.
BBE is blank ('...') in the packet for this verse; the comparison uses the other four versions.

history.note: [consider] Mention in the commentary that most of the commentators read 'is renewed' in this verse, against Rashi's 'passes at once'. (PS.90.6 Radak: 'וחלף זה מן לשון ... יחליפו כח ענין התחדשות'; Meiri: 'יציץ ויתחדש כמו אם יכרת ועוד יחליף'.)
[consider] Use 'we are terrified' in the literal layer, matching the gloss and the commentary. (PS.90.7 STEPBible 'we are terrified'; Ibn Ezra 'בבהלה'.)

agent_notes: The packet marks 'shatah' as Qere (Q(k)): per Radak and Meiri the word is written without the final heh and read with it, so the sense is unaffected. 'alumenu' is singular in form (lacking the plural yod), per Radak and Meiri; I render it as 'our hidden [sins]'. Rashi takes it as 'sins of our youth'; Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Metzudat David take it as 'hidden things'. I chose 'hidden'.

'hegeh' is rendered 'a sigh'. KJV 'a tale that is told' follows a different tradition and is not supported by the other four versions; the Hebrew word is a murmur or moan (Job 37:2 uses it of thunder; that is my own recollection, not a packet citation). Ibn Ezra, Rashi and Radak all read it as speech or utterance, so 'a sigh/murmur' stays within their range.
Убрано утверждение о сдвиге нумерации: в стихе 1 счёт KJV совпадает с ивритским, речь только о заглавии, которое KJV печатает отдельной строкой.

history.note: [should_fix] Replace «так что нумерация KJV во всём псалме сдвинута на единицу» with a plain statement such as «но счёт стихов от этого не меняется: стих 1 и в KJV начинается с «Господи»». agent_notes: rahbam — «спесь» (не «самая лучшая пора» Синодального): так сохранён горький оттенок корня «чваниться».

agent_notes: Комментарий упоминает числовую игру kaf-nun = 70 (Раши); в русском она не воспроизводима, оставлена как сообщение об иврите.

Комментарий: фраза про KJV теперь передаёт английское «let it repent thee» как цитату из KJV и даёт её смысл («да раскаешься Ты», буквально «пусть Тебе станет жаль»); итоговое замечание о Синодальном «умилосердись» сохранено.

agent_notes: dakka' — «раздавленное [состояние]» в буквальном слое, «растёртый в прах» в драматическом; Синодальный «в тление» — такая же абстракция, как KJV «destruction». Игру tashev / shuvu передаёт пара «Ты возвращаешь» / «возвратитесь».
